title: Your First Interface
story: You're building a chat app. You have Person types, Robot types, and soon maybe Pet types. You want one function that says hello to ANY of them — without writing three copies. You need a way to say 'anything that can greet' without caring what the thing actually is. Interfaces make this possible.
why: Interfaces let you write code that works with any type that has certain methods — the foundation of polymorphism, the most powerful abstraction in programming.
analogy: An interface is like a job description — 'must be able to greet.' Any candidate (type) that can do the job qualifies, regardless of whether they're a Person, Robot, or Alien. The hiring manager (generic function) only cares about the skill, not the species.
try_it: Add a `Robot` type with a `model: Str` field. Make it implement `greet()` by returning "Beep boop, model " + self.model. Pass a Robot to `introduce` — it should work immediately without changing `introduce`. Then try passing an Int — what error do you get?
tips: Any type that HAS the interface methods automatically satisfies the interface — no `implements` or `extends` keyword
`[T: Greetable]` constrains T to types that satisfy Greetable — the compiler enforces this
Interface satisfaction is checked at the CALL SITE — you'll see errors where you pass the wrong type, not where you define it
common_mistakes: Trying to add `implements Greetable` to a type — XIOM uses structural typing; just having the method is enough
Forgetting `self` parameter on methods — `fn greet() -> Str` on the interface means `fn greet(self) -> Str` on the type
Writing `fn introduce(thing: &Greetable)` instead of using generics — interfaces are constraints on generics, not standalone types
